l: Everything you write in Biblica stays on your device. It is never sent anywhere.
There are no accounts, no sign-in, no analytics, no advertising, no tracking and no cookies.
The app carries no code from anyone else and asks no other company’s servers for anything. Your browser is told to refuse if a page of the app ever tried.
Nobody can see your notes, your journal, your prayers or what you read: not the person who published this copy, not the people who wrote the app.
Because your writing exists only on your device, only you can keep it safe. Make a backup now and then.

p: Biblica keeps the following in your browser’s storage for this app, on this device and nowhere else:

l: your notes, highlights and the links you make between verses;
your reflections and your journal;
your daily list and, unless you turn it off, a note of what you prayed each day;
your novenas, intentions, saints and your own prayers;
your place in the Bible, in reading plans and in the day’s readings;
your settings, such as text size and calendar, and a few facts about this device’s copy: which version it last ran, when it last looked for an update and when you last made a backup;
what you mark in the examination of conscience and the date of your last confession, which are kept apart from the rest and left out of backups unless you ask for them;
a copy of the app itself, and of the Bible text and study material it has fetched, so that it works offline.

p: When the app restarts itself (after an update, a restore or erasing), your browser’s session storage holds which screen you were on, when it restarted and a message to show you. Session storage is emptied when the app is closed.

None of this is encrypted by the app. It is protected in the way everything in your browser is protected: by the lock on your device. Anyone who can unlock your phone and open Biblica can read what is in it. The app has no passcode of its own.
Nothing you write, ever. The only traffic is Biblica fetching its own files from the website it was installed from:

l: , when it is first installed and when it is updated.

The app asks the site for one small file when it is opened, when it is brought back into view (at most once in five minutes), every half hour while it stays open, and when a connection returns. If the site does not answer, or a release arrives incomplete, it asks again a few times over the next few minutes. “Check for updates” in Settings asks at once.

l.b: The Bible and study material, as they are needed.

l: When the app starts it fetches the books that the day’s readings and the prayers quote. It fetches a book when you first open it, the study material for a book when you first study it or read it with the Latin, and every book the first time you search. Each file is fetched once and read from your device after that.

p: These are ordinary downloads. They carry nothing you have written, no name and no identifier. They do carry what every web request carries: your internet address, a description of your browser, and which file was asked for. So the company that runs the server could tell roughly when someone at your address opens the app, and that the Book of Job was fetched on a certain day. It cannot tell what you do in the app, what you read once a book is on your device, or anything you write. If you would rather not leave even the trace of which books you open, save the whole Bible and the study material at once in Settings, under Storage; opening a book then fetches nothing.

blocks.h: Who runs the website, and what you are trusting

p: Biblica is not a service. It is a set of files, and the copy you are using is served by whoever published it. For a copy on GitHub Pages, the servers are run by GitHub, which like every web host keeps a record of requests under
. GitHub’s documentation describes no visitor records or statistics for the publisher of a Pages site, and the app adds none.

Everything on this page describes the app as it was written. The app updates itself from the site it was installed from, so whoever publishes the copy you use decides what code it runs, as with any website or app. If you do not know the publisher, or would rather trust nobody, the code is free to take: publish a copy of your own.

A few screens point to another website: the bishops’ outline of the Mass, the sites that carry the Liturgy of the Hours, and the sources credited in the app. These are marked as leaving the app and open only when you tap them. What that website learns is then between you and it. Biblica tells your browser not to pass on the address you came from.

A backup is a file made on your device when you ask for one. It holds what you have written and your settings. Biblica hands it to your phone’s share sheet or its downloads folder, and where it goes from there is your choice. If you put it in a cloud service, that service’s terms apply to it. The file is plain text, not encrypted, so keep it somewhere you trust. Confession notes are left out unless you turn that on.

l: It does not ask for your location, contacts, camera, microphone or photos.
It sends no notifications.
It shows no advertising and contains nothing from an advertising or analytics company.
It loads no fonts, scripts or images from other sites.
It does not send anything you write to an AI service or to anyone else.
It does not sell or share information, because it has none.

p: Settings, Your data, Erase everything removes all your writing and every setting from this device at once. It leaves the app’s own files and the Bible text and study material saved for offline use; those hold nothing you wrote, though which books are saved could show which you had opened. To remove those as well, clear this site’s data in your browser. On an iPhone, deleting the app from the home screen does the same. A backup you made earlier is not affected: delete that file yourself if you want it gone.

blocks.h: What is outside the app’s control

l: Whether your phone’s own backups include browser storage is decided by its maker, not by Biblica.
A browser extension, or a device that has been tampered with, can read any page you open, this one included.
On a shared device or browser profile, anyone who uses it can open the app.

Browsers may clear a website’s storage that has not been used for a long time. Apps added to the home screen are normally spared, and Biblica asks the browser to protect its storage, but a backup is the only sure protection.

p: Biblica collects nothing from anyone, of any age.
Every file of the app can be read as it is served, and a copy on GitHub Pages is published from a public repository. The first page,

, carries a content security policy that forbids the app’s pages from loading anything from, or sending anything to, any site but their own, and your browser enforces it. The one part a page’s policy does not cover is the service worker, the small program that keeps the app available offline; the project’s tests check that it, like every other script, names no other site. Your browser’s network inspector will show every request the app makes.

l: Biblica is free. It is offered as it is, with no promise that it is free of mistakes.
It is an aid to prayer and study. It is not an official book of the Church, and it does not replace the sacraments, your parish or a priest.
What you write in it is yours and stays on your device. Keeping a backup is up to you.
The code may be reused under the MIT licence. The texts and data that come from others keep their own terms, and a few short excerpts from the current Missal are not free to reuse at all.

p: Biblica is free software together with old texts that are in the public domain. There is no account, no payment and no service behind it: nobody is obliged to keep a copy online, to correct it or to answer questions about it. By using it you accept these terms. If you do not, please do not use it.

blocks.h: Not an official book of the Church

p: Biblica has no imprimatur and has not been reviewed or approved by any bishop, by a bishops’ conference or by the Holy See.

l: The Bible is the Douay-Rheims in Bishop Challoner’s revision. The Mass readings are shown in that translation, which is not the one read at Mass.

The prayers are given in their long-established forms. The current English translations of the Roman Missal and of the Liturgy of the Hours are under copyright. The Liturgy of the Hours is not included. Of the Missal only short excerpts are given, in the Mass companion: the people’s responses, the priest’s short lines, and the first words of the longer prayers.

The Mass companion is a guide to following the Mass. It is not the Missal, and it does not carry the full approved text of the ordinary form in English. Its English of the older Mass is a translation for following the Latin, not an approved text.

The calendar, the holy days of obligation and the days of fasting and abstinence are worked out by the app for the United States or for the General Roman Calendar. They can be wrong, and dioceses differ. Your parish and your diocese are the authority.

p: The examination of conscience, the guides to prayer, the notes on the saints and the commentary of the Fathers are aids. They are no substitute for a confessor, a spiritual director or the teaching of the Church, and nothing in the app is medical or psychological advice. If you are in distress or in danger, contact your local emergency number or someone you trust.

The app contains mistakes. Texts were typed, matched and selected partly by machine; the historical notes were written for this project and only some have been checked against sources; verse numbers can be a verse off in a few books. The release notes (
) list what is known. Treat the app as a prompt to look something up, not as the last word.

Your notes, journal and everything else you write belong to you and exist only on your device. They can be lost if the device is lost or reset, if the app is deleted, or if the browser clears its storage. Nobody can recover them for you. Make backups, and keep them somewhere safe: a backup file is plain text that anyone can read.

items: Updates now arrive by themselves: the app looks for a new version when it is opened and when it comes back into view, and Settings can check at once and say what it found.
A release is taken whole or not at all: if a file is missing from the site, or left over from an earlier version, the app stays as it is and says which.
The daily list has no boxes to tick. It is a list of what you mean to pray today, each a tap away, with a quiet word once you have prayed it.
Prayers can repeat on certain weekdays, on a day of the month, on a first Friday or Saturday, once a year, or only in certain months or seasons.
A Mass companion: the liturgy at a glance and a text to follow, for the ordinary form and for the traditional Latin Mass.
A plain privacy statement, terms of use, the licence and a page of sources, all inside the app.
Settings shows how much room the app takes on this device and lets you free it.
A page on the Divine Office: what it is, what of it the app already carries, and where to pray the whole of it.
A study screen for any passage: the Latin Vulgate, cross-references and what the Fathers of the Church wrote about it.
Reflections that can cite any number of passages, and a journal kept with the evening examen.
A page for every day: what is celebrated, whether Mass is of obligation, and what happened on this date.
Your own saints, with their feast days on Today.
The Litany of the Sacred Heart, in English and Latin.
Daily prayers, the Rosary, the Stations of the Cross, Lectio Divina and the examen.
Novenas, intentions, an examination of conscience and a guide to confession.
A library of prayers in English and Latin.
The Douay-Rheims Bible, the liturgical calendar and the readings of the day, offline.
Notes, highlights and links between verses, with backup and restore.
